learningObjective: Explain why the community invests in a stable, versioned operator set at the framework-compiler boundary.
stem: Which statement best captures the design rationale for putting a stable, versioned operator set (StableHLO) at the framework-compiler boundary?

options.text: It decouples the release cycles of frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) and compilers (XLA, IREE, ...): each side can evolve independently as long as they respect the StableHLO version compatibility contract, avoiding an O(frameworks × compilers) integration matrix and enabling shared optimization work.

It forces every framework to adopt identical implementation details, so any two frameworks that consume StableHLO produce bit-identical outputs on all hardware, eliminating framework-level differences in numerical results.
It replaces the need for framework-specific tracing tools; any framework that emits StableHLO no longer needs its own graph capture mechanism (TorchDynamo, JAX's tracer, TF's tf.function).
It exists primarily to give the compiler backend access to Python source code so that Python-native optimizations (e.g., decorator rewriting) can be applied at the compiler level.

explanation: The core design motivation for StableHLO (and similar interchange IRs) is to decouple the release cadence of ML frameworks from that of compiler backends. Without a stable contract, each new framework release risks breaking downstream compilers and vice versa — leading to a combinatorial integration burden (O(frameworks × compilers)). A versioned operator set with compatibility guarantees lets each side ship independently and share common optimization/backend infrastructure.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: portability contract that reduces combinatorial integration cost.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: StableHLO does not mandate bit-identical numerics across frameworks/backends.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: frameworks still need their own capture tools; StableHLO is only the target IR.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: StableHLO is not tied to Python source access.

assumptions: OpenXLA StableHLO design motivations as documented.
nonImplications: Does not imply StableHLO removes the need for framework-specific optimizations.
Does not imply full portability of performance — hardware/backend differences still matter.

distractorRationales.B: Confuses semantic portability with bit-identical numerics.
distractorRationales.C: Confuses interchange IR with tracing tools.
distractorRationales.D: Wrong claim about Python source dependency.
